blocks.text: The graph of the function \(f(x) = \cot x\) with domain \(\{x \mid x \in \mathbb{R} \wedge x \ne n\pi,\ n \in \mathbb{Z}\}\) and range \((-\infty, \infty)\) is shown in Figure 9.14.

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: \(\cot x = \frac{\cos x}{\sin x}\), so the points where \(\sin x = 0\) (\(x = n\pi\)) are removed; they are the vertical asymptotes. Unlike \(\csc x\) and \(\sec x\), \(\cot x\) takes every real value: on each branch it falls from \(+\infty\) to \(-\infty\). So its range is all of \(\mathbb{R}\).

blocks.alt: Graph of y = cot x for x from minus 2 pi to 2 pi. Dashed vertical asymptotes at x = minus 2 pi, minus pi, 0, pi and 2 pi. Between each pair of neighbouring asymptotes the curve falls from plus infinity to minus infinity, crossing the x-axis at the odd multiples of pi over 2. A dashed horizontal line y = 2 cuts every branch once.
blocks.caption: Figure 9.14: graph of \(y = \cot x\) from \(-2\pi\) to \(2\pi\) (original drawing after the textbook's figure)

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: On the \(x\)-axis of the book's Figure 9.14 (marked in steps of \(\frac{\pi}{3}\)), the point \(-\pi\) is labelled '\(\pi\)': the minus sign is missing. Our drawing marks the axis in steps of \(\frac{\pi}{2}\) and labels \(-\pi\) correctly.

Clearly from the graph it follows that cotangent function is not bijective because the line \(y = 2\) intersects the graph at many points. So, we restrict the domain of \(f(x) = \cot x\) to the interval \((0, \pi)\), then the function with restricted domain i.e., \(f : (0, \pi) \to (-\infty, \infty)\) becomes one-one and onto that is invertible and is called principal cotangent function. The inverse cot x function is defined by

blocks.text_alt: y equals inverse cotangent of x if and only if x equals cotangent of y

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: Why \((0, \pi)\) and not \(\left(-\frac{\pi}{2}, \frac{\pi}{2}\right)\) as for tangent? \(\cot x\) is not defined at \(x = 0\), which sits in the middle of \(\left(-\frac{\pi}{2}, \frac{\pi}{2}\right)\). On \((0, \pi)\) there is one complete branch: \(\cot x\) falls steadily from \(+\infty\) to \(-\infty\), taking every real value exactly once.
The domain of \(\cot^{-1} x\) is \((-\infty, \infty)\) and range of \(\cot^{-1} x\) is \((0, \pi)\).
The graph of the function \(\cot : (0, \pi) \to (-\infty, \infty)\) is shown in Figure 15(a) and graph of \(\cot^{-1} : (-\infty, \infty) \to (0, \pi)\) is shown in Figure 9.15(b).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The book refers to 'Figure 15(a)'. The figure is Figure 9.15(a).

blocks.alt: Principal branch of y = cot x on the open interval 0 to pi. The curve falls from plus infinity near the y-axis, passes through (pi over 2, 0) and goes down to minus infinity near the dashed asymptote x = pi.
blocks.caption: Figure 9.15(a): graph of \(y = \cot x\) from 0 to \(\pi\) (original drawing after the textbook's figure)

blocks.alt: Graph of y = inverse cotangent of x for all real x. The curve decreases from near the dashed line y = pi on the far left, passes through (0, pi over 2), and approaches the x-axis on the far right without touching it.
blocks.caption: Figure 9.15(b): graph of \(y = \cot^{-1} x\) (original drawing after the textbook's figure)

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: Reflecting Figure 9.15(a) in \(y = x\) gives Figure 9.15(b): \(\left(\frac{\pi}{2}, 0\right) \to \left(0, \frac{\pi}{2}\right)\). The vertical asymptotes \(x = 0\) and \(x = \pi\) become the horizontal asymptotes \(y = 0\) and \(y = \pi\). So \(\cot^{-1} x\) is always strictly between 0 and \(\pi\); it is never negative. For example \(\cot^{-1}(-1) = \frac{3\pi}{4}\), not \(-\frac{\pi}{4}\).

blocks.title: Example 2
steps:
Given: three expressions, each a trigonometric function of an inverse trigonometric value.
To find: the value of each expression.
Method: work from the inside out. First find the inner angle (the principal value of the inverse function, inside its principal range), then apply the outer function to that angle.

(i) Name the inner angle
\[\tan^{-1}(-\sqrt{3}) = y\]
\[\tan y = -\sqrt{3}\]
\[y \in \left(-\dfrac{\pi}{2}, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right)\]
Why: by definition \(y = \tan^{-1} x \iff x = \tan y\), and the principal value of \(\tan^{-1}\) lies in \(\left(-\frac{\pi}{2}, \frac{\pi}{2}\right)\).

(i) Find \(y\)
\[\tan y = -\sqrt{3} = \tan\left(-\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)\]
\[y = -\dfrac{\pi}{3}\]
So \(\tan^{-1}(-\sqrt{3}) = -\frac{\pi}{3}\).
Why: \(\tan\frac{\pi}{3} = \sqrt{3}\) and tangent is odd, so \(\tan\left(-\frac{\pi}{3}\right) = -\sqrt{3}\); \(-\frac{\pi}{3}\) is inside the principal range. (\(\frac{2\pi}{3}\) also has tangent \(-\sqrt{3}\) but is outside the range.)

(i) Apply secant
\[\sec\left[\tan^{-1}(-\sqrt{3})\right]\]
\[= \sec\left(-\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right) = \dfrac{1}{\cos\frac{\pi}{3}}\]
\[= \dfrac{1}{1/2} = 2\]
Why: \(\sec\theta = \frac{1}{\cos\theta}\), and cosine is even, so \(\cos\left(-\frac{\pi}{3}\right) = \cos\frac{\pi}{3} = \frac{1}{2}\).

(ii) Name the inner angle
\[\cos^{-1}\left(-\dfrac{1}{2}\right) = y\]
The book prints: First, we find the angle 1, whose cosine is \(-\sqrt{3}\). It means the angle \(y\) whose cosine is \(-\frac{1}{2}\) (see the Book correction below).
\[\cos y = -\dfrac{1}{2},\quad y \in [0, \pi]\]
Why: the principal value of \(\cos^{-1}\) lies in \([0, \pi]\).

(ii) Find \(y\)
\[\cos y = -\dfrac{1}{2} = \cos\dfrac{2\pi}{3}\]
\[y = \dfrac{2\pi}{3}\]
Why: \(\cos\frac{\pi}{3} = \frac{1}{2}\) and \(\cos(\pi - \theta) = -\cos\theta\), so \(\cos\frac{2\pi}{3} = -\frac{1}{2}\); \(\frac{2\pi}{3} \in [0, \pi]\).

(ii) Apply cotangent
\[\cot\dfrac{2\pi}{3} = \dfrac{\cos\frac{2\pi}{3}}{\sin\frac{2\pi}{3}}\]
\[= \dfrac{-1/2}{\sqrt{3}/2} = -\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\]
Why: \(\cot\theta = \frac{\cos\theta}{\sin\theta}\), and \(\sin\frac{2\pi}{3} = \sin\frac{\pi}{3} = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\) (second quadrant, sine positive).

(iii) Name and find the inner angle
\[\sin^{-1}\left(\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right) = y\]
\[\sin y = \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2},\ y \in \left[-\dfrac{\pi}{2}, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right]\]
\[\sin y = \sin\dfrac{\pi}{3} \Rightarrow y = \dfrac{\pi}{3}\]
Why: \(\sin\frac{\pi}{3} = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\) and \(\frac{\pi}{3}\) is in the principal range of \(\sin^{-1}\).

(iii) Apply cosecant
\[\csc\left[\sin^{-1}\left(\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\right)\right]\]
\[= \csc\dfrac{\pi}{3} = \dfrac{2}{\sqrt{3}}\]
Why: \(\csc\theta = \frac{1}{\sin\theta}\), so it is the reciprocal of \(\frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\). (Shortcut: \(\csc(\sin^{-1} t) = \frac{1}{t}\) whenever \(t \ne 0\).)

Check:
(i) \(\cos\left(-\frac{\pi}{3}\right) = \frac{1}{2}\), reciprocal 2.
(ii) \(\cos^{-1}(-0.5) \approx 2.0944\) and \(\cot 2.0944 \approx -0.5774 = -\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\).
(iii) \(\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}} \approx 1.1547 = \frac{1}{0.8660}\).
book_errors: First, we find the angle 1, whose cosine is \(-\sqrt{3}\).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: Example 2(ii): the book prints 'First, we find the angle 1, whose cosine is \(-\sqrt{3}\).' It should read 'First, we find the angle \(y\), whose cosine is \(-\frac{1}{2}\).' (\(-\sqrt{3}\) cannot be a cosine at all, since \(|\cos y| \le 1\).) The working and the answer \(-\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\) are correct.

blocks.title: Teaching note
Example 3
blocks.problem: Find the domain of the following functions (i) \(f(x) = \cos^{-1}(3x - 1)\) (ii) \(g(x) = \sin^{-1}\left(\frac{x^{2} - 5}{4}\right)\) (iii) \(h(x) = \sec^{-1}(\ln x)\)
steps:
Given: three functions built from inverse trigonometric functions.
To find: the domain of each.
Method: an inverse trigonometric function only accepts inputs from its own domain: \(\cos^{-1}\) and \(\sin^{-1}\) need the input in \([-1, 1]\); \(\sec^{-1}\) needs the input in \((-\infty, -1] \cup [1, \infty)\). So we put the inside expression into that condition and solve the inequality for \(x\).

(i) Write the condition
The inverse cosine function \(\cos^{-1} x\) is defined for all \(x\) such that \(-1 \le x \le 1\). So we need
\[-1 \le 3x - 1 \le 1\]
Why: the input of \(\cos^{-1}\) here is \(3x - 1\).

(i) Solve
\[0 \le 3x \le 2\]
\[0 \le x \le \dfrac{2}{3}\]
\[x \in \left[0, \dfrac{2}{3}\right]\]
The book ends: Hence, the domain of \(f(x) = \cos^{-1}(3x - 1)\) is \(\left[0, \frac{2}{3}\right]\) such that \(-1 \le x \le 1\). The last phrase is stray (see the Book correction below); the domain is just \(\left[0, \frac{2}{3}\right]\).
Why: add 1 to all three parts, then divide all three by 3 (a positive number, so the inequality signs stay the same).

(ii) Write the condition
\[-1 \le \dfrac{x^{2} - 5}{4} \le 1\]
\[-4 \le x^{2} - 5 \le 4\]
\[1 \le x^{2} \le 9\]
Why: \(\sin^{-1}\) needs its input in \([-1, 1]\); multiply all parts by 4, then add 5.

(ii) Split into two conditions
\[x^{2} \ge 1 \Rightarrow x \le -1 \text{ or } x \ge 1\]
i.e. \(x \in (-\infty, -1] \cup [1, \infty)\), and
\[x^{2} \le 9 \Rightarrow (x - 3)(x + 3) \le 0\]
i.e. \(x \in [-3, 3]\).
Why: \(x^{2} \ge 1\) means \(|x| \ge 1\). A product of two factors is \(\le 0\) only between (or at) its roots \(-3\) and \(3\).

(ii) Take the common part
The intersection of the two results gives
\[x \in [-3, -1] \cup [1, 3]\]
The book writes: Thus, the domain of \(f(x) = \sin^{-1}\left(\frac{x^{2} - 5}{4}\right)\) is \([-3, -1] \cup [1, 3]\). The function is called \(g(x)\) in the question.
Why: both conditions must hold at the same time, so we keep only the \(x\) that lie in both sets.

(iii) Write the conditions
\(\sec^{-1}\) is defined on \((-\infty, -1] \cup [1, \infty)\), so
\[\ln x \ge 1 \ \text{ or } \ \ln x \le -1\]
Also \(\ln x\) itself exists only for \(x > 0\).
Why: the input of \(\sec^{-1}\) is \(\ln x\), and a logarithm needs a positive argument. This second condition is the one the book forgets.

(iii) Solve
\[\ln x \ge 1 \Rightarrow x \ge e\]
\[\ln x \le -1 \Rightarrow 0 < x \le e^{-1} = \dfrac{1}{e}\]
The book writes \(x \ge e\) or \(x \le \frac{1}{e}\), and so \(x \in \left(-\infty, \frac{1}{e}\right] \cup [e, \infty)\).
Why: \(e^{x}\) is increasing, so applying it to both sides keeps the inequality: \(x = e^{\ln x} \ge e^{1}\) or \(x \le e^{-1}\). The \(x\) must still be positive.

(iii) The domain
\[x \in \left(0, \dfrac{1}{e}\right] \cup [e, \infty)\]
Why: we join the two pieces, keeping only positive \(x\). For example \(x = -1\) is not allowed: \(\ln(-1)\) does not exist.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text:
Example 3 has three slips.
(i) The conclusion adds 'such that \(-1 \le x \le 1\)' after \(\left[0, \frac{2}{3}\right]\). This phrase is stray; the domain is \(\left[0, \frac{2}{3}\right]\).
(ii) The conclusion names the function \(f(x)\); in the question it is \(g(x) = \sin^{-1}\left(\frac{x^{2} - 5}{4}\right)\). The domain \([-3, -1] \cup [1, 3]\) is correct.
(iii) The book gives the domain of \(h(x) = \sec^{-1}(\ln x)\) as \(\left(-\infty, \frac{1}{e}\right] \cup [e, \infty)\). But \(\ln x\) is defined only for \(x > 0\), so the correct domain is \(\left(0, \frac{1}{e}\right] \cup [e, \infty)\).

blocks.title: Example 4
blocks.problem: Prove that: (i) \(\csc^{-1} x = \sin^{-1}\frac{1}{x},\ x \in (-\infty, -1] \cup [1, \infty)\) (ii) \(\sec^{-1} x = \cos^{-1}\frac{1}{x},\ x \in (-\infty, -1] \cup [1, \infty)\) (iii) \(\cot^{-1} x = \tan^{-1}\frac{1}{x},\ x \in (0, \infty)\)
steps:
Given: the definitions of \(\csc^{-1}\), \(\sec^{-1}\), \(\cot^{-1}\).
To prove: each one equals an inverse of the reciprocal function at \(\frac{1}{x}\).
Method: let the left side be \(y\), turn it into an ordinary trigonometric equation with the definition, use a reciprocal identity, and read it back as an inverse function. Then check that \(y\) lies in the principal range of the new inverse function.

Proof (i): set up
Let \(\csc^{-1} x = y\), then
\[x = \csc y\]
Why: definition \(y = \csc^{-1} x \iff x = \csc y\), with \(y \in \left[-\frac{\pi}{2}, 0\right) \cup \left(0, \frac{\pi}{2}\right]\).

Proof (i): reciprocal
\[\sin y = \dfrac{1}{x}\]
\[y = \sin^{-1}\left(\dfrac{1}{x}\right)\]
Hence
\[\csc^{-1} x = \sin^{-1}\left(\dfrac{1}{x}\right)\]
Why: \(\csc y = \frac{1}{\sin y}\), so \(\sin y = \frac{1}{x}\) (\(x \ne 0\)). Since \(|x| \ge 1\), \(\left|\frac{1}{x}\right| \le 1\), so \(\sin^{-1}\frac{1}{x}\) exists; and \(y\) lies in \(\left[-\frac{\pi}{2}, \frac{\pi}{2}\right]\), the principal range of \(\sin^{-1}\), so it is exactly \(\sin^{-1}\frac{1}{x}\).

Proof (ii)
Let \(\sec^{-1} x = y\), then \(x = \sec y\).
\[\cos y = \dfrac{1}{x}\]
\[y = \cos^{-1}\left(\dfrac{1}{x}\right)\]
Hence \(\sec^{-1} x = \cos^{-1}\left(\frac{1}{x}\right)\).
Why: \(\sec y = \frac{1}{\cos y}\); \(y \in \left[0, \frac{\pi}{2}\right) \cup \left(\frac{\pi}{2}, \pi\right]\) lies inside \([0, \pi]\), the principal range of \(\cos^{-1}\).

Proof (iii)
Let \(\cot^{-1} x = y\), then \(x = \cot y\).
\[\tan y = \dfrac{1}{x}\]
\[y = \tan^{-1}\left(\dfrac{1}{x}\right)\]
Hence \(\cot^{-1} x = \tan^{-1}\left(\frac{1}{x}\right)\).
Why: \(\tan y = \frac{1}{\cot y}\). For \(x > 0\), \(y = \cot^{-1} x\) lies in \(\left(0, \frac{\pi}{2}\right)\), which is inside \(\left(-\frac{\pi}{2}, \frac{\pi}{2}\right)\), the principal range of \(\tan^{-1}\). That is why the book states \(x \in (0, \infty)\).
blocks.answer: Hence proved: \(\csc^{-1} x = \sin^{-1}\frac{1}{x}\), \(\sec^{-1} x = \cos^{-1}\frac{1}{x}\) for \(|x| \ge 1\), and \(\cot^{-1} x = \tan^{-1}\frac{1}{x}\) for \(x > 0\).

blocks.title: Teaching note
blocks.text: Why does (iii) need \(x > 0\)? For \(x < 0\), \(\cot^{-1} x\) lies in \(\left(\frac{\pi}{2}, \pi\right)\), outside the range of \(\tan^{-1}\). Example: \(\cot^{-1}(-1) = \frac{3\pi}{4}\), but \(\tan^{-1}(-1) = -\frac{\pi}{4}\). For negative \(x\) the correct relation is \(\cot^{-1} x = \pi + \tan^{-1}\frac{1}{x}\). Parts (i) and (ii) need no such restriction because the ranges already fit.

blocks.title: Example 5
blocks.problem: Prove that (i) \(\sin^{-1} x + \cos^{-1} x = \frac{\pi}{2},\ x \in [-1, 1]\) (ii) \(\csc^{-1} x + \sec^{-1} x = \frac{\pi}{2},\ x \in (-\infty, -1] \cup [1, \infty)\) (iii) \(\tan^{-1} x + \cot^{-1} x = \frac{\pi}{2},\ x \in (-\infty, \infty)\)
steps:
Given: \(x\) in the stated domains.
To prove: each pair of 'co-functions' adds up to \(\frac{\pi}{2}\).
Method: let \(\sin^{-1} x = y\), write \(x = \sin y\) as a cosine using \(\cos\left(\frac{\pi}{2} - \alpha\right) = \sin\alpha\), and read it back as \(\cos^{-1}\).

(i) Set up
Let \(\sin^{-1} x = y\)
\[x = \sin y = \cos\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2} - y\right)\]
Why: definition of \(\sin^{-1}\) (\(y \in \left[-\frac{\pi}{2}, \frac{\pi}{2}\right]\)), and the co-function identity \(\cos\left(\frac{\pi}{2} - \alpha\right) = \sin\alpha\).

(i) Read back as \(\cos^{-1}\)
\[x = \cos\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2} - y\right)\]
\[\cos^{-1} x = \dfrac{\pi}{2} - y\]
Why: from \(-\frac{\pi}{2} \le y \le \frac{\pi}{2}\) we get \(0 \le \frac{\pi}{2} - y \le \pi\), the principal range of \(\cos^{-1}\). The book does not say this, but it is what makes the step valid.

(i) Rearrange
\[\cos^{-1} x + y = \dfrac{\pi}{2}\]
\[\cos^{-1} x + \sin^{-1} x = \dfrac{\pi}{2}\]
Hence, \(\sin^{-1} x + \cos^{-1} x = \frac{\pi}{2}\).
Why: add \(y\) to both sides and put back \(y = \sin^{-1} x\).

(ii) Our working (the book says 'Similarly, we can prove (ii) and (iii)')
By Example 4, for \(|x| \ge 1\):
\[\csc^{-1} x + \sec^{-1} x\]
\[= \sin^{-1}\dfrac{1}{x} + \cos^{-1}\dfrac{1}{x}\]
\[= \dfrac{\pi}{2}\]
Why: \(t = \frac{1}{x}\) lies in \([-1, 1]\), so part (i) applies to \(t\).

(iii) Our working
Let \(\tan^{-1} x = y\), \(y \in \left(-\frac{\pi}{2}, \frac{\pi}{2}\right)\).
\[x = \tan y = \cot\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2} - y\right)\]
\[\cot^{-1} x = \dfrac{\pi}{2} - y\]
\[\tan^{-1} x + \cot^{-1} x = \dfrac{\pi}{2}\]
Why: co-function identity \(\cot\left(\frac{\pi}{2} - \alpha\right) = \tan\alpha\); and \(0 < \frac{\pi}{2} - y < \pi\), the principal range of \(\cot^{-1}\).
blocks.answer: Hence proved: \(\sin^{-1} x + \cos^{-1} x = \frac{\pi}{2}\), \(\csc^{-1} x + \sec^{-1} x = \frac{\pi}{2}\), \(\tan^{-1} x + \cot^{-1} x = \frac{\pi}{2}\) on the stated domains.

blocks.title: Example 6
steps:
Given: the angle \(\cos^{-1}\frac{7}{25}\).
To prove: it equals \(\csc^{-1}\frac{25}{24}\).
Method: call the angle \(\alpha\), find \(\sin\alpha\) from \(\cos\alpha\) with \(\sin^{2}\alpha + \cos^{2}\alpha = 1\), then take the reciprocal to get \(\csc\alpha\).

Name the angle
Let \(\cos^{-1}\frac{7}{25} = \alpha\)
\[\cos\alpha = \dfrac{7}{25},\quad \alpha \in \left[0, \dfrac{\pi}{2}\right]\]
Why: the range of \(\cos^{-1}\) is \([0, \pi]\), and since \(\frac{7}{25} > 0\), the angle is in the first quadrant.

Choose the sign
\[\sin\alpha = \dfrac{24}{25}\]
Why: \(\alpha \in \left[0, \frac{\pi}{2}\right]\), where sine is not negative.

Take the reciprocal
\[\csc\alpha = \dfrac{25}{24}\]
\[\alpha = \csc^{-1}\dfrac{25}{24}\]
Why: \(\csc\alpha = \frac{1}{\sin\alpha}\). Also \(\alpha\) lies in \(\left(0, \frac{\pi}{2}\right]\), inside the principal range of \(\csc^{-1}\), so \(\alpha\) is exactly the principal value \(\csc^{-1}\frac{25}{24}\) (the book skips this check).

Conclusion
\[\cos^{-1}\dfrac{7}{25} = \csc^{-1}\dfrac{25}{24}\]
Why: both are equal to the same angle \(\alpha\).

Check:
7, 24, 25 is a Pythagorean triple: \(7^{2} + 24^{2} = 49 + 576 = 625 = 25^{2}\). In a right triangle with adjacent side 7, opposite side 24 and hypotenuse 25, \(\cos\alpha = \frac{7}{25}\) and \(\csc\alpha = \frac{25}{24}\). Numerically both angles are about 1.2870 rad.

blocks.title: Example 7
blocks.problem: Without using calculator find the value of \(\sin\left[\frac{1}{2}\tan^{-1}\frac{4}{3}\right]\).
steps:
Given: the angle \(\tan^{-1}\frac{4}{3}\).
To find: the sine of half of it.
Method: name the angle \(\alpha\); from \(\tan\alpha = \frac{4}{3}\) build the point \((3, 4)\) to get \(\sin\alpha\) and \(\cos\alpha\); then use the half-angle identity \(\sin\frac{\alpha}{2} = \sqrt{\frac{1 - \cos\alpha}{2}}\), which needs only \(\cos\alpha\).

Name the angle
Let \(\tan^{-1}\frac{4}{3} = \alpha\)
\[\tan\alpha = \dfrac{4}{3}\]
Why: definition of \(\tan^{-1}\). Since \(\frac{4}{3} > 0\), \(\alpha \in \left(0, \frac{\pi}{2}\right)\).

Find \(r\)
Here, \(x = 3\), \(y = 4\)
\[r = \sqrt{x^{2} + y^{2}}\]
\[= \sqrt{3^{2} + 4^{2}} = \sqrt{25} = 5\]
Why: \(\tan\alpha = \frac{y}{x}\), so we may take the point \((3, 4)\) on the terminal arm of \(\alpha\); \(r\) is its distance from the origin.

Find \(\sin\alpha\) and \(\cos\alpha\)
The book prints: So, \(\sin\alpha = \frac{3}{5}\) and \(\cos\alpha = \frac{4}{5}\). These two values are swapped (see the Book correction below). Correctly:
\[\sin\alpha = \dfrac{y}{r} = \dfrac{4}{5}\]
\[\cos\alpha = \dfrac{x}{r} = \dfrac{3}{5}\]
Why: \(\sin\alpha = \frac{y}{r}\), \(\cos\alpha = \frac{x}{r}\). Test: \(\frac{\sin\alpha}{\cos\alpha} = \frac{4/5}{3/5} = \frac{4}{3} = \tan\alpha\), while the book's pair would give \(\frac{3}{4}\).

Half-angle identity
\[\sin\dfrac{\alpha}{2} = \sqrt{\dfrac{1 - \cos\alpha}{2}}\]
Why: it comes from \(\cos\alpha = 1 - 2\sin^{2}\frac{\alpha}{2}\). We take the positive root because \(\frac{\alpha}{2} \in \left(0, \frac{\pi}{4}\right)\), where sine is positive.

Substitute \(\cos\alpha = \frac{3}{5}\)
\[\sin\dfrac{\alpha}{2} = \sqrt{\dfrac{1 - \frac{3}{5}}{2}}\]
\[= \sqrt{\dfrac{2/5}{2}} = \sqrt{\dfrac{1}{5}}\]
\[= \dfrac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\]
Why: \(1 - \frac{3}{5} = \frac{2}{5}\), and \(\frac{2}{5} \div 2 = \frac{1}{5}\). In this line the book itself uses \(\cos\alpha = \frac{3}{5}\), the correct value, so its result is right.

Check:
\(\sin^{2}\frac{\alpha}{2} = \frac{1}{5}\) gives \(\cos\frac{\alpha}{2} = \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}\). Then \(\sin\alpha = 2\sin\frac{\alpha}{2}\cos\frac{\alpha}{2} = 2 \cdot \frac{1}{\sqrt{5}} \cdot \frac{2}{\sqrt{5}} = \frac{4}{5}\), as found above.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: Example 7: with \(x = 3\), \(y = 4\), \(r = 5\) the book writes \(\sin\alpha = \frac{3}{5}\) and \(\cos\alpha = \frac{4}{5}\). These are swapped: \(\sin\alpha = \frac{y}{r} = \frac{4}{5}\) and \(\cos\alpha = \frac{x}{r} = \frac{3}{5}\). The next line of the book already uses \(\cos\alpha = \frac{3}{5}\), so the final answer \(\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}\) is correct.

blocks.title: Key points
blocks.text:
1. \(\cot x\): domain \(\mathbb{R} - \{n\pi\}\), range \(\mathbb{R}\). Principal cotangent function: \(\cot : (0, \pi) \to (-\infty, \infty)\).
2. \(y = \cot^{-1} x \iff x = \cot y\); domain \((-\infty, \infty)\), range \((0, \pi)\).
3. To evaluate an expression like \(\sec[\tan^{-1} a]\), find the inner principal value first, then apply the outer function.
4. For a domain question, put the inside expression into the domain of the inverse function and solve; remember any extra condition such as \(x > 0\) for \(\ln x\).
5. \(\csc^{-1} x = \sin^{-1}\frac{1}{x}\), \(\sec^{-1} x = \cos^{-1}\frac{1}{x}\) (\(|x| \ge 1\)); \(\cot^{-1} x = \tan^{-1}\frac{1}{x}\) (\(x > 0\)).
6. \(\sin^{-1} x + \cos^{-1} x = \csc^{-1} x + \sec^{-1} x = \tan^{-1} x + \cot^{-1} x = \frac{\pi}{2}\).

blocks.title: Common mistake
blocks.text:
1. Answering \(\cot^{-1}\) of a negative number with a negative angle: \(\cot^{-1}(-\sqrt{3}) = \frac{5\pi}{6}\), not \(-\frac{\pi}{6}\).
2. Using \(\cot^{-1} x = \tan^{-1}\frac{1}{x}\) for negative \(x\): it holds only for \(x > 0\).
3. Picking an inner angle outside the principal range, e.g. \(\tan^{-1}(-\sqrt{3}) = \frac{2\pi}{3}\).
4. In domain questions, forgetting the domain of the inner function (like \(x > 0\) for \(\ln x\)).
5. Mixing up \(\sin\alpha\) and \(\cos\alpha\) from a point \((x, y)\): \(\sin\alpha = \frac{y}{r}\), \(\cos\alpha = \frac{x}{r}\).
